analysis.title: Global Space & Defense Tech Summit: Key Takeaways
key_insights: Deutsche Bank's fifth annual Global Space & Defense Tech Summit in NYC hosted nearly 100 companies and 500 attendees. The bank says investor interest was the highest it has seen.

Launch panel (Firefly, Impulse, Rocket Lab and others) flagged an intensifying launch shortage. SpaceX is described as essentially phasing out Falcon 9 in 2029, which panelists say alternatives such as Neutron, Eclipse, Nova and Terran R cannot fully replace.

Panelists said there could be up to a 100 Falcon 9 equivalent launch deficit by 2030 if Starship capacity is dedicated exclusively to internal needs such as Starlink. It is also unclear whether New Glenn can add material capacity given its manifest for Amazon LEO and the US government.

On orbital data centers, Rocket Lab has had discussions with hyperscalers about collaborating. Impulse questioned the economics for anyone who cannot match Starship's future launch costs of $200-400/kg. Firefly cited space-based supercomputing opportunities building on its Scitec acquisition.

D2D panel (AST SpaceMobile, Viasat and others) said the opportunity is shifting from proving the technology to executing at scale. Spectrum, satellites, launch access and MNO partnerships are the key enablers, and the panel viewed MNO-led D2D joint ventures in the US and Europe positively.
D2D infrastructure could also address broader MSS opportunities, including government and sovereign applications and Enterprise IoT.
Launch demand currently exceeds supply, so D2D providers want access to multiple launch partners. The panel expects non-SpaceX industry capacity to become less constrained around 2029.

AST SpaceMobile's Blacklift reusable rocket is expected to launch up to five BlueBird satellites per mission from late 2028. Deutsche Bank sees it as a step toward launch self-reliance and lower costs but thinks the timing is optimistic.

European panel (OHB, PLD, Seraphim, SWISSto12) said governments feel urgency to rebuild regional space capability. The German government and ESA are urging domestic investment and ownership of key space assets, procurement is being simplified, and governments are more willing to award large contracts to start-ups.

Germany is targeting €35bn of space-related defense spending by 2030, and OHB believes the benefits are just starting to flow through. SWISSto12 sees growing appetite among small and mid-sized European nations for sovereign constellations.

Europe's launch shortage and dependence on US capacity is a central concern. PLD Space noted Europe relied heavily on Falcon 9 after Soyuz. OHB and another panelist also cited a lack of local launch infrastructure (reliance on Kourou) and a fragmented supply chain.

2027 markers for European names: OHB begins executing its defense-centric backlog, one launch company targets a maiden Miura 5 flight toward mid-year, and SWISSto12 rolls out next-gen payloads after reaching positive EBITDA this year.

Spacecraft panel (CesiumAstro, Intuitive Machines, Muon and others) named defense and sovereign demand as the main volume drivers, with faster procurement cycles and quicker contracting in tactical comms, ISR and missile defense. Intuitive Machines said GEO satellite demand is surging for the first time in a decade.

Most spacecraft panelists see fully integrated satellites, rather than just the bus or payload, as the differentiator, alongside the shift to software-defined digital payloads. CesiumAstro and MDA have moved to full solutions.

Optical terminals remain supply-constrained, as do certain propulsion types and radiators. Muon sees a significant launch constraint through 2030 and MDA says launch now comes up directly in customer conversations.

On orbital data centers, spacecraft panelists doubted the economics more than the engineering and questioned whether any vehicle other than Starship offers a viable path. CesiumAstro sees edge compute as a potential opportunity.

Space and Defense convergence panel (SDA fireside, HawkEye 360, Voyager, Karman) was constructive on US midterm results, citing bipartisan support, programs in the base budget and limited reliance on supplementals. Panelists saw Golden Dome as an umbrella of capabilities rather than a single program at risk.

SDA said its constraint is execution rather than funding. Encryption and optical terminals are bottlenecks and launch could become one, which may mechanically favor smaller payloads. Tranche 2 is in production, Tranche 3 is in critical design review, and Tranche 4 adds sensor accuracy and edge compute. Value is shifting toward data and compute.

M&A: Karman wants to buy technology rather than revenue, Voyager is doing tuck-ins in fragmented areas, and HawkEye 360 focuses on signal processing and prefers optical and SAR data through partnerships and APIs.

Drone panel (Neros, NextVision, Ondas, Unusual Machines) framed the drone revolution as an industrialization and supply-chain story. Competitive advantage depends on the ability to produce, replenish, iterate and sustain unmanned systems at scale.

Domestic drone industrial base is approaching the capacity needed for current DoW demand but remains unprepared for another large-scale contingency. Gaps remain in thermal and optical sensors and memory, and one country supplied about 85% of the US drone supply chain two years ago.
Counter-UAS is already about 50% of Unusual Machines' business. Traditional defense primes were viewed as complementary because they focus on lower-volume, exquisite systems.

Next-gen propulsion panel (Firehawk, Rocketdyne) said rising demand across munitions, solid rocket motors and space makes scale and schedule as important as technology. Firehawk's automated thermoplastic propellant process aims to cut production cycles from months to days and could reach about 400,000 units annually at scale.

Propulsion capacity expansion is constrained by capital, demand visibility and supply-chain readiness, which raises the importance of multi-year agreements. Space demand is strong across the DoW, primes and commercial customers such as Amazon.

Geospatial panel (BlackSky, Umbra) reported healthy demand driven by geopolitical conflicts. BlackSky cited Gen-3 moving from pilots to long-term contracts and a $3bn sovereign pipeline, while the SAR player offers day-and-night, weather-agnostic imaging at lower cost.

AI is reshaping both geospatial business models. BlackSky wants a data-use flywheel where customers build models and query feeds with AI agents instead of buying raw data, and is focused on its financial profile via lower-cost purpose-built satellites.

Deutsche Bank lists eight Top Picks in the report: SpaceX, Firefly Aerospace, Rocket Lab, AST SpaceMobile, Viasat, Intuitive Machines, MDA Space and BlackSky. No ratings or price targets are legible in the extracted text.
Disclosure: Deutsche Bank and/or its affiliates is acting as advisor to Rocket Lab on the potential acquisition of Iridium.

sector_views.rationale: Launch demand exceeds supply, Falcon 9 is being phased out in 2029, and panelists see a possible deficit of up to 100 Falcon 9 equivalents by 2030. Capacity is expected to ease from around 2029.
Opportunity is shifting from proving technology to scaling, helped by MNO-led JVs. Launch access is the near-term execution challenge.
Bipartisan budget support, faster procurement and strong demand for drones, counter-UAS and solid rocket motors. Industrial capacity and supply chains are the constraint.

Governments are urging sovereign space capability, with Germany targeting €35bn of space-related defense spending by 2030. Launch dependence on the US and a fragmented supply chain remain constraints.

earnings_insights: SWISSto12 said it is already EBITDA positive this year and is aiming for +50% sales growth in 2027 (management target as relayed in the report).
OHB expects to begin executing its defense-centric backlog in 2027 and believes the benefits of European space spending are just starting to flow through.
BlackSky highlighted significant growth from Gen-3 moving from pilot programs to long-term contracts, supported by a $3bn sovereign pipeline.
Counter-UAS already represents about 50% of Unusual Machines' business per the panel.
risk_factors: Launch shortage: a possible deficit of up to 100 Falcon 9 equivalents by 2030 if Starship capacity is reserved for internal needs.
New Glenn may not add material capacity given its manifest for Amazon LEO and the US government.
Orbital data center economics depend on launch costs approaching Starship's future $200-400/kg.
Supply constraints in optical terminals, certain propulsion types, radiators, thermal and optical sensors and memory.
Encryption is a bottleneck for SDA programs and launch could become one.
Europe's dependence on US launch capacity, limited local infrastructure and a fragmented supply chain.
Deutsche Bank believes AST SpaceMobile's Blacklift timing is optimistic.
Capital, demand visibility and supply-chain readiness limit propulsion capacity expansion.
geopolitical: Geopolitical conflicts are described as pushing European governments to seek regional technology control and sovereign space infrastructure.
Panelists said geopolitical conflicts are driving healthy demand for geospatial intelligence, including international demand.
Germany and ESA are urging regional players to invest in domestic space infrastructure and own key space assets.
Panelists said the domestic US drone industrial base remains unprepared for another large-scale contingency.

tension_points.bull_case: Rocket Lab has held discussions with hyperscalers about collaborating, Firefly sees opportunities in space-based supercomputing, and CesiumAstro sees edge compute as a potential opportunity.
tension_points.bear_case: Impulse questioned the economics for anyone who cannot match Starship's future launch costs of $200-400/kg, and spacecraft panelists doubted the economics more than the engineering and whether any vehicle other than Starship offers a viable path.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Launch costs staying well above Starship's future $200-400/kg, since panelists said ultra-low launch cost is required to deploy at scale.

tension_points.bull_case: The panel expects capacity constraints to ease over time, with non-SpaceX industry capacity less constrained around 2029 and new rockets possibly flying by the end of the decade.
tension_points.bear_case: Falcon 9 is being phased out in 2029, alternatives may not replace it, New Glenn's manifest is full, and the history of launch suggests multi-year cadence ramps, leaving a possible 100 Falcon 9 equivalent deficit by 2030.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Starship capacity being dedicated exclusively to internal needs such as Starlink would widen the deficit, per panelists.
